# What this is

`docdesigner` renders R Markdown into publication-quality PDFs. A **style** is a
small file of design tokens — typefaces, colours, spacing, rules — that the
engine turns into a typeset page. The promise is *same content, any style*: you
point one document at a different style and it re-typesets, without your touching
a word of the prose.

Twelve styles ship, in two sets. `academic` holds `minimal`, `nature`,
`methods`, `demography`, `ssrn`, `sociology` and `ajs`. `public` holds `policy`,
`government`, `economist`, `atlantic` and `humanities`.

This document was itself typeset by docdesigner, in the `methods` style.

# Setup

You need R, a LaTeX installation providing `xelatex`, and pandoc. RStudio bundles
pandoc; TinyTeX and MiKTeX both work for LaTeX. If you have knitted an R Markdown
document to PDF before, you already have all three.

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jncohen/docdesigner")

library(docdesigner)
designer_check()      # reports anything missing from the toolchain
designer_styles()     # the twelve styles, with their sets
```

If `designer_check()` reports a problem, fix that before going further. Nearly
every confusing failure downstream is a missing `xelatex` or a missing font.

**Please tell us how this step went even if it went fine** — how long it took,
and whether anything was unclear. Installation is the step most likely to lose a
new user, and it is the one we can least easily test ourselves.

# What to try

Three tasks, in order. The second is the important one.

## Render something

Make a new R Markdown document, or take any small one you have, and put this at
the top:

```yaml
---
title: "Anything at all"
author: "Your Name"
output:
  docdesigner::pdf:
    style: minimal
---
```

Knit it. That is the whole interface — one line names the style. If this
produces a PDF, the package works on your machine.

## Render a real document of your own

This is what we most need. Take a genuine paper, report or memo of yours — the
messier the better, ideally one with sections, tables, figures, footnotes and a
bibliography — and render it. Then change that one `style:` line and render it
again, three or four times:

```yaml
output:
  docdesigner::pdf:
    style: nature      # then sociology, humanities, ssrn, ...
```

We want to know whether **your content survives the switch**. Tables that
overflow the page, figures that land in the wrong column, citations that stop
resolving, headings that collide with the running head, code that runs off the
edge — that is the failure class we cannot find on our own test documents,
because our test documents are tidy and yours are real.

Note that `nature` and `economist` are two-column. Wide tables and long code
lines are the usual casualty there, and we would like to know how badly.

## Install a style set

```r
designer_install_set("academic")
designer_sets()
```

Sets install to your R user directory and survive package updates. This checks
that distribution works from a machine that is not ours.

# What we most want to hear

Beyond outright breakage, the thing we cannot see from here is **where you got
stuck**. Specifically:

- What did you have to look up, guess at, or read twice?
- What did you expect to exist and not find?
- Did anything behave differently from how you assumed it would?
- How long did the whole thing take, start to finish?

"I assumed X and it turned out to be Y" is a more useful report than most bug
reports. Please send those even when nothing was broken.

# What we already know about

The engine is finished and tested, and the styles are now substantially
designed: every setting a style declares is rendered, and the two styles that
previously looked generic — `economist` and `government` — have the full-bleed
masthead bands their designs are built around.

**So yes, please do comment on how they look.** Earlier drafts of these
instructions asked you not to; that is out of date.

Three things are genuinely still unfinished. Reporting them costs you time and
tells us nothing new:

**1. No shipped style puts the title on its own page.** The engine can do it —
set `title.page_break_after: true` in a style — but every style we ship opens
with a title block at the head of the body. The richer title-page furniture
(institution, series and report numbers, a formal author block) is the next
piece of engine work.

**2. `policy` is being redesigned** from scratch, so judge it lightly.

**3. Validation reports a handful of "not yet implemented" settings.** That
list is accurate: those are recognised but not yet acted on. It is a roadmap,
not a fault.

One thing that is intentional rather than unfinished: **fonts substitute.**
Proprietary typefaces are replaced by bundled open ones — XITS for Times, EB
Garamond for oldstyle, Source Serif 4 for various. A style being "not quite the
real typeface" is expected. A substitution that looks *wrong at the size used*
is worth telling us about.

# How to report

Email **josephncohen@gmail.com**, one message per problem, with
`docdesigner alpha` in the subject line.

What makes a report actionable, in rough order of value:

1. **Attach the PDF**, or a screenshot of the part that went wrong. We cannot
   judge a layout problem from a description.
2. **Which style**, and whether other styles do the same thing. "`sociology`
   only" and "all twelve" are different bugs.
3. **A small `.Rmd` that reproduces it.** If your document is confidential, cut
   it down until it is not — that usually localises the problem anyway.
4. **The output of `designer_check()`**, and of `sessionInfo()`.
5. **What you expected instead.**

If something failed to install, send the full console output, including the
error. That is usually enough on its own.
